summary: This San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library fact sheet summarizes key information about the brown bear (Ursus arctos), covering its taxonomy, physical measurements, range, habitat, IUCN status, behavior, diet, reproduction, life expectancy in managed care, and feature facts. It notes the brown bear is the most widespread bear in the world and has the lowest reproduction rate of any mammal. The sheet was updated in 2015 with minor updates in 2019, and the page was last updated March 6, 2024.
one_line: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance fact sheet on the brown bear (Ursus arctos), covering its biology, range, diet, reproduction, and conservation status.
key_facts: Brown bear (Ursus arctos) was described by Linnaeus in 1758 and belongs to order Carnivora, family Ursidae.
Male brown bears weigh 130-550 kg (287-1213 lb); females weigh 80-250 kg (176-551 lb).
Brown bear head/body length is 1-2.8 m (3.3-9.2 ft) for both sexes, with shoulder height up to 1.5 m (5 ft).
Brown bear range includes Europe, Middle East, Asia, northwestern U.S., and western Canada.
Brown bears inhabit the widest variety of habitats of any bear species, from sea level to 5,000 m (16,404 ft).
IUCN Status for the brown bear is Least Concern (2016 assessment).
Wild brown bear population is more than 200,000.
Brown bear gallop speed is 56 km/hr (35 mp/h).
Brown bear diet is more carnivorous than that of American and Asiatic black bears.
Female brown bears reach sexual maturity at about 3.5 years, with first cubs at 4-8 years; males at about 5.5 years.
Brown bear gestation lasts 6-7 months, with litter size commonly 2-3 and up to 4.
Median life expectancy in managed care is about 22 years in males and 27 years in females.
Shoulder hump, concave snout and smaller ears distinguish the Brown Bear from the Black Bear.
Mother bears with young are extremely defensive and will attack male bears.
In a 2010 enrichment strategy, exhibit spaces were connected for two young grizzly bears and an elderly Manchurian brown bear at the San Diego Zoo.
